title: Geopolitical zone disparities and correlates of minimum adequate antenatal care utilization in Nigeria: A multilevel analysis of the 2024 NDHS
content:
by Abdirasak Sharif Ali, Uthman Okikiola Adebayo, Mohamed Abdirahim Omar, Olalekan John Okesanya, Yahye Sheikh Abdulle Hassan, Jamilu Sani, Mohamed Mustaf Ahmed

Background

Antenatal care (ANC) is a fundamental component of maternal healthcare that is critical for improving maternal and neonatal outcomes. Although the 2016 World Health Organization (WHO) model recommends a minimum of eight contacts, the four-or-more-visit indicator remains widely used in Demographic and Health Survey (DHS)-based monitoring and permits comparability with previous Nigerian and regional evidence. This study examined geopolitical zone disparities and individual- and community-level correlates of minimum adequate antenatal care utilization, defined as four or more antenatal care visits, using the 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS).

Methods

This cross-sectional study used data from the 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey. The study population comprised women aged 15–49 years who had a live birth within the five years preceding the survey and had complete information on the analytic variables (unweighted n = 12,797; sum of normalized sampling weights = 13,442.7; 6.3% missingness excluded). Survey weights were normalized by dividing the Demographic and Health Survey sampling weight by 1,000,000, and the descriptive analyses accounted for clustering and stratification. Unweighted multilevel mixed-effects logistic regression was used to account for the hierarchical structure of women nested within 1,355 clusters and to identify individual- and community-level factors associated with four or more antenatal care visits in the last pregnancy.

Results

The national weighted prevalence of four or more antenatal care visits was 52.9% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 51.0%–54.7%; unweighted n = 6,824 [53.3%]). Marked regional heterogeneity was observed, with the South West zone recording the highest prevalence (88.7%, 95% CI: 85.2%–91.4%) and the North West zone recording the lowest (40.2%, 95% CI: 37.0%–43.4%). Multilevel analysis showed that the cluster-level variance on the latent scale in the null model was 2.877, yielding an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 46.7% (95% CI: 43.5%–49.8%). Significant individual-level correlates included higher education (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 3.93, 95% CI: 3.04–5.09, p < 0.001), belonging to the rich wealth group (aOR = 2.37, 95% CI: 1.99–2.82, p < 0.001), and facility delivery (aOR = 3.28, 95% CI: 2.93–3.67, p < 0.001), interpreted as a continuum-of-care correlate rather than a temporally prior predictor. At the community level, relative to urban residence, rural residence (aOR = 0.80, 95% CI: 0.68–0.94, p = 0.007) was associated with lower odds of utilization. Relative to the North West reference zone, South West residence (aOR = 1.93, 95% CI: 1.43–2.61, p < 0.001) and North East residence (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.27–1.86, p < 0.001) were associated with higher odds of utilization, while North Central residence (aOR = 0.75, 95% CI: 0.61–0.92, p = 0.005) was associated with lower odds of antenatal care utilization after adjusting for individual-level composition.

Conclusion

Slightly more than half of women in the analytic sample achieved four or more antenatal care visits, with substantial disparities across geopolitical zones and socioeconomic groups. The observed associations support attention to underserved populations and continuity of maternal healthcare. The four-visit indicator does not measure adherence to the current WHO eight-contact recommendation, which requires a separate analysis.
